claims.claim: A budget is a plan, expressed in numbers, for how a business will use its cash and other resources in a future period; budgets are quantitative plans for the future.
Budgeting serves planning, which develops future objectives, and controlling, which monitors whether those objectives are being met.
A master budget combines operating budgets, which plan day-to-day revenues and expenses, with financial budgets, which plan cash inflows and outflows and the budgeted balance sheet.
The revenue (sales) budget states expected sales in units and price for the period and is the foundation that the other operating budgets build on.
The selling and administrative expense budget lists the variable and fixed nonproduction expenses expected in the period, such as salaries and other nonmanufacturing costs.
The cash budget totals expected cash receipts, subtracts cash payments from available cash, and shows whether the business will fall below its minimum cash balance and need financing.
A static budget is built on a single level of activity and stays fixed, while a flexible budget adjusts planned costs to the actual level of activity so results can be compared fairly.

A budget is a detailed financial plan that sets targets and allocates resources for a period, typically fixed for a year, whereas a forecast predicts future outcomes from current and historical data and is updated frequently.
Comparing actual results with the budget shows where a problem may exist, and budgets are revised as conditions change, including rolling budgets that are continuously updated.
The budgeting process includes establishing objectives and targets, developing the detailed budget, compiling and revising the budget model, and committee review and approval.

conflictingEvidence: Sources organize budget components differently: CFI names operating, capital, and cash budgets, while OpenStax groups a master budget into operating budgets (sales, production, selling and administrative) and financial budgets (cash, capital asset, budgeted balance sheet). The lesson follows the task's revenue/expense/cash naming and treats capital budgets as out of scope, so no factual conflict arises.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Accounting, Volume 2: Managerial Accounting, 7.1 Describe How and Why Managers Use Budgets
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read via Internet Archive capture (2026-03-07) because openstax.org blocks curl. Supports: budgets as quantitative plans for the future; a budget as a plan for when and how cash and other resources will be used; the most common budget period of one year; planning versus controlling; the master budget containing operating and financial budgets; the sales budget as the foundation for other operating budgets; the financial budget consisting of the cash budget, budgeted balance sheet, and capital expense budget; rolling budgets; and the ethical tension around reporting results that meet budget goals.
